result: Shamsi accepted one build with changes and rejected three. The rules added after round 6 held in every build: no breadcrumbs, no links above the heading, no page zones, the internal logo, and a heading that follows the reader's choices. The main content starts as high as in round 6's revised pages or higher. The rejections are about one choice: three builds put the category list or the explanation in a sidebar on the activity charts page, which narrows the charts and leaves an empty column beside a long page.

A.notes: Eight rules on tokens. Sorts with a select, a checkbox and a Sort button instead of the sort bar.

B.notes: Heading levels skip from h1 to h3 on all sections (axe). One class used with no rule. No footer.

C.notes: Six rules on tokens (placeholder, category rows, chart row). Uses the sort bar as GET submit buttons.

D.notes: Nine rules on tokens. Sorts with a select and a Sort button instead of the sort bar.

patterns: All four: the internal logo, Staff reports in the header, the two-level navigation with the compact filter bar, headings such as 'Submissions and holds, all of cs', no breadcrumbs, no page zones.
Three of four used a sidebar on activity charts (B, C, D); round 6's agents had considered one and rejected it.
No build used a tooltip, popover or modal for the explanation or the category list; the transcripts do not mention them.
Two of four used the sort bar. A and D said the documented sort bar uses type=button, which cannot send a GET form, so they used a select.
B and C put a one-line 'About these figures' in an accordion.
Primary content top at 1440 by 900: all sections 180 to 228px (round 6 after: 228 to 298); activity charts 423 to 540px (round 6 after: 417 to 577).
Predictions: 1 right (no breadcrumb or link above the heading). 2 wrong (two of four used the sort bar). 3 right (the main content starts no lower). 4 wrong (no build accepted without changes).
findings: The sidebar guidance says when a sidebar is appropriate but not what it costs: it narrows the main content, and beside a long main column it leaves empty space. Three builds took it for the category list.

Secondary content has one named home in the main-content rule ('below the main content or in an accordion'), so agents never weigh a popover, a modal or a footnote, and they put a one-line note in an accordion.
The sort bar demo uses type=button, so two agents could not see how to make it work in a GET form and fell back to a select with a Sort button.
next: Say what a sidebar costs and when it is wrong; give secondary content a short list of homes with a test for each; show the sort bar as GET submit buttons; then run the reports once more.
